chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Fed at the Center

lessons.title: Case Study: The 2013 Taper Tantrum and India's Rupee Defense

body.text: The 2013 taper tantrum is the canonical case study in this course. A mere hint from the Fed, not even an actual rate hike, was enough to trigger a violent reversal of capital from India, and the RBI's response to it wrote a playbook India still leans on today.

children.text: By early 2013, years of Fed QE had pushed global investors to chase yield in emerging markets, India included. India's own macro position was already stretched: a current account deficit near a record high, financed partly by portfolio flows that can reverse in weeks rather than the foreign direct investment that tends to stay for years. That combination, an economy dependent on flows that can leave quickly, is precisely what made India vulnerable to what came next.

body.title: The Taper Tantrum, Month by Month

events.title: Bernanke's Taper Hint
events.description: Fed Chair Ben Bernanke tells Congress the Fed could start slowing, or "tapering," its bond purchases in the coming meetings if the economy kept improving. No policy had actually changed yet; only the future path of QE was in question.

events.title: Capital Flees Emerging Markets
events.description: Global investors sell EM debt and equity in anticipation of tighter dollar liquidity ahead. India, alongside Indonesia, Brazil, Turkey and South Africa, sees some of the sharpest outflows and currency pressure, later nicknamed the "Fragile Five" by market commentary.

events.title: The Rupee Hits Its Low
events.description: The rupee falls to an intraday low near ₹68.8 per dollar, down roughly a fifth from where it started the year, as FPI outflows and dollar demand overwhelm the RBI's initial defenses.

events.title: Raghuram Rajan Takes Over as RBI Governor
events.description: Rajan is appointed RBI Governor in the middle of the crisis and moves quickly with a package of measures aimed directly at stabilizing the rupee and rebuilding reserves.

events.title: The Rupee Stabilizes
events.description: The FCNR(B) swap scheme and related measures draw in dollar inflows, reserves rebuild, and the rupee recovers a meaningful part of its losses over the following months.

body.text: Dates and levels above are drawn from widely reported 2013 coverage and are approximate. Confirm precise figures against RBI's own historical data before citing them.

A current account deficit is not automatically dangerous. It becomes dangerous when it is financed by hot money, portfolio flows chasing yield, rather than by foreign direct investment or stable long-term capital. Portfolio money can leave in weeks. A factory built with FDI cannot. India's 2013 current account deficit, close to a record high relative to GDP that year, was financed heavily by exactly the kind of flows that reversed the moment the Fed's future path looked less generous.

children.text: The FCNR(B) Swap: Buying Dollars Without Burning Reserves

Simply raising interest rates to defend the rupee has a cost: it slows an already-strained economy. Rajan's RBI instead leaned on a more targeted tool: a special window letting banks raise FCNR(B) deposits, foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians, and swap the dollars with the RBI at a subsidized forward rate. Because the swap cost was subsidized, banks could offer NRIs an attractive effective return, drawing in a large pool of dollar deposits without the RBI having to sell down its own reserves or hike rates as aggressively as a pure defense would have required.

body.label: FCNR(B) Swap Scheme Inflows, 2013
body.context: The scheme drew in a large pool of dollar deposits from non-resident Indians, materially rebuilding RBI reserves and helping stabilize the rupee within a few months, according to RBI's own widely cited figures.

children.text: 2013 vs 2022: Why the Next Fed Tightening Cycle Hurt Less

body.title: India's Position Entering Two Fed Tightening Shocks

columns.label: 2013 Taper Tantrum
points: Current account deficit near a record high relative to GDP
Forex reserves a few hundred billion dollars, a comparatively thin buffer
India grouped among the market-labeled "Fragile Five" as a standout vulnerable economy

columns.label: 2022 Global Tightening Cycle
points: Current account deficit far smaller relative to GDP than in 2013
Forex reserves roughly double the 2013 level, a much larger buffer
India held up comparatively well versus other emerging markets despite one of the fastest Fed hiking cycles on record

body.text: Comparative figures are approximate and directional, meant to show the scale of improvement in India's external position, not precise year-by-year data. Check RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement and Ministry of Finance current account data for exact figures.

body.title: Why Not Just Raise Rates?
body.scenario: In September 2013, the newly appointed RBI Governor had two broad options to defend a collapsing rupee: raise interest rates sharply across the board, or launch a targeted scheme like the FCNR(B) swap aimed specifically at drawing in NRI dollar deposits.
body.prompt: From a liquidity standpoint, why might a targeted scheme be preferable to a blunt, economy-wide rate hike during a currency crisis?
body.modelAnswer: A blunt, economy-wide rate hike defends the currency by making rupee assets more attractive to everyone, but it also raises borrowing costs for the whole economy at a moment when growth is already fragile, and it does not directly address the underlying dollar shortage driving the crisis. A targeted scheme like the FCNR(B) swap goes straight at the actual problem: too few dollars relative to demand. By subsidizing the swap cost for banks raising NRI deposits, the RBI drew in a large, specific pool of new dollar inflows without needing to hike rates as aggressively economy-wide, rebuilding reserves and calming the rupee while limiting collateral damage to domestic growth.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why were current account deficit countries like India hit harder than others during the 2013 taper tantrum?
options: Because they had no central bank to respond
Because their deficits were financed heavily by portfolio flows that could reverse quickly, unlike more stable FDI
Because they had pegged their currencies to the dollar
Because they had no foreign exchange reserves at all
body.explanation: A current account deficit financed by portfolio flows chasing yield is far more vulnerable to a sudden reversal than one financed by foreign direct investment, which is much stickier. When the Fed's future policy path looked less generous, portfolio money left quickly, hitting deficit countries like India especially hard.

points: The 2013 taper tantrum was triggered by a mere hint about future Fed policy, not an actual rate hike, showing how forward guidance alone can move global liquidity.
India was especially vulnerable because its current account deficit was financed heavily by portfolio flows, which can reverse far faster than foreign direct investment.
The RBI's FCNR(B) swap scheme drew in roughly $34 billion in NRI dollar deposits, rebuilding reserves and stabilizing the rupee without needing an economy-wide rate hike alone.

India entered the 2022 global tightening cycle with a much stronger external position, a smaller current account deficit and roughly double the forex reserves of 2013, which is a major reason that cycle was comparatively less disruptive.
A currency defense built around targeted, dollar-specific tools can be more effective and less costly to growth than blunt, economy-wide rate hikes alone.
